intro: Twenty two lines of complaint after the superscription, and the whole psalm is one sick man's inventory: flesh, bones, loins, wounds, heart, eyes. For a learner it is the best place in the book to collect body nouns carrying the first person suffix, because nearly every line supplies one. Watch verse 16, where the psalm stops describing and starts addressing, and notice that nothing is cured by the end. The last thing asked for is speed.

stichs.en: A psalm of David.
To bring to remembrance.

verses.summary: The heading gives a purpose rather than an occasion. It files the psalm as something brought before God, not merely something sung.

stichs.en: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your rage,
and do not chasten me in Your wrath.

verses.summary: Almost word for word the opening of Psalm 6, with one noun of anger swapped for another. The request is not that the discipline stop, only that it not be delivered hot.

stichs.en: For Your arrows have sunk into me,
and Your hand has come down upon me.

verses.summary: Two pictures of one blow: arrows already landed, and a weight still pressing. The speaker takes the illness as God's own doing, which is what gives him standing to argue with it.

stichs.en: There is no soundness in my flesh because of Your indignation;
there is no peace in my bones because of my sin.

verses.summary: Two clauses with identical shape, each naming a cause. The first blames God's indignation, the second the speaker's own sin, and the psalm never separates the two again.

stichs.en: For my iniquities have passed over my head;
like a heavy burden they are too heavy for me.

verses.summary: Water and weight inside one verse: guilt first floods above the head, then sits on the shoulders. Sin is described entirely in the vocabulary of physics.

stichs.en: My wounds stink and fester
because of my folly.

verses.summary: The most physical line here. Both verbs of rot come before the noun they belong to, so the smell arrives before the wound is even named.

stichs.en: I am bent, I am bowed down very low;
all the day I go about darkened.

verses.summary: Posture used as diagnosis. Bent, bowed and walking in mourning, and sustained all day rather than at a set hour of prayer.

stichs.en: For my loins are filled with burning,
and there is no soundness in my flesh.

verses.summary: The catalogue circles back to the body and repeats the phrase from verse 4 word for word. The repetition is how the psalm shows that nothing has moved.

stichs.en: I am numb and crushed to the last degree;
I have roared from the groaning of my heart.

verses.summary: The one loud verb in the psalm, the word used of a lion, and it rises out of a heart that is only groaning. Noise and exhaustion turn out to be the same event.

stichs.en: My Lord, all my longing is before You,
and my sighing is not hidden from You.

verses.summary: The turn to address. Everything catalogued so far is declared already visible, which converts the rest of the psalm from a report into an appeal.

stichs.en: My heart goes round and round,
my strength has left me;
and the light of my eyes, even that is gone from me.

verses.summary: Three systems failing in one line: circulation, strength, sight. The light of the eyes leaving is the standard biblical idiom for a body giving out.

stichs.en: Those who love me and my companions stand back from my affliction,
and my kinsmen have stood far off.

verses.summary: The illness becomes social. Two verbs of standing frame the verse so that nobody in it moves closer, and the thing they keep away from is the affliction itself.

stichs.en: Those who seek my life lay snares,
and those who look for my harm speak of ruin and deceits,
all the day they mutter.

verses.summary: The empty space left by the friends fills with enemies. Their muttering runs all day, set deliberately against the all day of verse 7.

stichs.en: But I am like a deaf man, I do not hear,
and like a mute who does not open his mouth.

verses.summary: The answer to the plotting is silence. Deaf and mute are chosen here rather than suffered, since a man who cannot hear is a man who need not reply.

stichs.en: I have become like a man who does not hear,
and in whose mouth there are no arguments.

verses.summary: The comparison is repeated and then explained. The closing noun is a legal word, so the silence is specifically a refusal to plead his own case.

stichs.en: For it is for You, O LORD, that I have waited;
You will answer, my Lord my God.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. The silence was not weakness: the defence has been handed to someone else, and three divine names arrive in the space of two lines.

stichs.en: For I said: let them not rejoice over me;
when my foot slips they magnify themselves against me.

verses.summary: What he fears is not death but their pleasure. A slipping foot is the ordinary image for a life losing its footing, and they are watching for exactly that.

stichs.en: For I am ready to stumble,
and my pain is before me continually.

verses.summary: A strange thing to admit inside a plea: he says he is ready to fall. The pain stands in front of him, using the same word he used in verse 10 for standing before God.

stichs.en: For I declare my iniquity,
I am anxious because of my sin.

verses.summary: Confession stated flatly, in the present. Declaring the iniquity and worrying about it sit side by side, so admission is not presented as relief.

stichs.en: But my enemies are alive and strong,
and those who hate me falsely are many.

verses.summary: The contrast drawn is health, not morality. His enemies are described as vigorous, and the word for falsehood is left hanging at the end of the line.

stichs.en: Those who repay evil in place of good accuse me,
in place of my pursuing good.

verses.summary: The exchange is spelled out with the same preposition twice: evil for good, hostility for the pursuit of good. Doing right is given as the cause of the attack.

stichs.en: Do not forsake me, O LORD my God;
do not be far from me.

verses.summary: The plea returns to the volitive negative that opened the psalm in verse 2, and what it asks for is presence rather than a cure.

stichs.en: Hurry to my help,
my Lord, my salvation.

verses.summary: Four words, and the last is a title rather than a request. The psalm ends with no cure, holding on to speed and to a name.

pardes.body: A body, then a social circle, then a courtroom. Verses 2 to 11 catalogue the illness from the inside; verses 12 and 13 pull back far enough to show friends withdrawing and enemies moving into the gap; verses 14 to 21 are the speaker's conduct under that pressure, which turns out to be silence, confession, and no self defence. The hinge is {{16.3}}, the verb of waiting, and it explains everything before it, because a man who has handed his case over has no reason to argue his own corner. Nothing is healed by the end. The final two verses ask only that God stay close and come fast.

The opening of verse 2 is the opening of Psalm 6 with one word of anger substituted for another, close enough that the two are regularly noted together. {{4.1}}, glossed here as soundness, is a rare noun from the root meaning whole or complete, so the complaint is not that something hurts but that nothing in him is intact. {{7.6}} means darkened, and the same word is used elsewhere of people in mourning dress and of a sky going black, which is why the line can be read as clothing or as mood. And {{1.2}}, the only real word in the superscription, shares a root with the memorial portion burned from the grain offering in Leviticus 2, which lets the psalm present itself as an offering rather than as a song.

The reading tradition takes the superscription at its word: a psalm said to bring something to remembrance is one a person recites when he wants his own case raised, which turns the whole catalogue of symptoms into evidence submitted rather than complaint vented. The silence of verses 14 and 15 is the part most often expanded. Plainly read, a man too weak to answer keeps quiet; read the other way, the silence is deliberate, a decision not to defend himself in front of people because the defence has already been filed in verse 16. On that reading the psalm is not really about illness. It is about what to do while under accusation. In Christian liturgy it is counted among the seven penitential psalms, which is a fact about its reception rather than about its text.

Read mystically the catalogue stops being medical. The psalm counts downward through flesh, bones, loins, wounds, heart and eyes, and in the kabbalistic idiom the body is the lower map of a whole structure, so organs that have stopped working are describing channels that have stopped conducting. {{11.1}}, a heart going round in circles, and the light leaving the eyes in the same verse are the two directions of that flow slackening at once. This is also why the request of verse 22 makes sense exactly as it stands: not repair, but that the source not withdraw, since a channel with nothing above it has nothing left to carry.
